Gyurov signed a ten-year security agreement with Ukraine in Kyiv on 30 March 2026 without a prior National Assembly vote authorising the signature.

No National Assembly vote authorised the signature. A mandate was, however, requested: caretaker PM Glavchev wrote to the Assembly on 18 December 2024 and Speaker Kiselova refused to table it on 19 December 2024, holding that signing fell within the government's competence. The claim is accurate as to the absence of a mandate but omits that one was formally sought and refused by the speaker.
The omission matters: it turns 'the speaker declined to table it' into 'he never asked'.
The agreement binds Bulgaria for ten years.
The signed text runs for ten years and enters into force on signature, though it characterises its content as political commitments rather than treaty obligations.
The agreement went through the National Assembly and the speaker returned it, saying the power to sign lay with the government.

A mandate request was submitted through the speaker in December 2024 and she declined to table it, citing government competence. That is not the same as the agreement being 'discussed in parliament', which did not happen; the 'returned' part matches the record.
Compresses a refusal to table into a parliamentary deliberation.
By signing, Bulgaria committed itself to take part in the coalition of the willing.
The text only says the parties value the coalition's work and confirm engagement with its activities. It creates no formal membership and no automatic commitment to participate.
The gap between 'we value its work' and 'we are committed to join' is the whole dispute.
When Gyurov signed, the National Assembly was sitting and could have been asked.
No record was located of the Assembly's session calendar on 30 March 2026, so whether it was sitting on the signing date could not be established.
Would be settled by the Assembly's register of sittings for March 2026.
It is a framework agreement under which implementing contracts may be signed.
The text provides that authorised institutions of the parties may conclude implementing and technical agreements.
Every contract concluded under the framework requires National Assembly ratification.

The agreement itself contains no ratification clause; it is expressly placed outside the Vienna Convention and framed as political commitments. Whether Bulgarian constitutional law independently requires ratification for particular implementing instruments was not established.
The speaker may be relying on Article 85 of the constitution, which is a separate question from what the text says.
The agreement nowhere provides for Bulgarian soldiers to be sent to Ukraine.
A full-text search of the 20-page signed text finds no reference to Bulgarian military personnel being deployed to Ukraine; the only personnel references concern Ukrainian service members.
The agreement opens the way for Bulgarian companies to take part in Ukraine's reconstruction.
The text supports cooperation on technology, innovation and joint testing; an explicit reconstruction clause was not located in the evidence gathered.
Needs the full text checked clause by clause.
The coalition of the willing is currently training member-state soldiers as peacekeeping forces for after the war.
No primary record of the coalition's current training programme was located.
The parties that nominated Gyurov voted for Bulgaria's participation in the coalition of the willing.
No parliamentary vote on coalition-of-the-willing participation was located in the evidence.
Would be settled by the Assembly voting record.
The agreement is equally binding as an international treaty.

The text places itself outside the Vienna Convention and describes its content as political commitments, which is the opposite of treaty bindingness. Kyiv's own description of it as fixing 'clear obligations' does not change the instrument's self-declared status.
There is not a single binding sentence in the agreement.

The instrument self-describes as political commitments, excludes the Vienna Convention, and contains no enforcement or ratification machinery. 'Not a single binding sentence' is rhetorical, but the substance holds.
The Botash contract was signed by a caretaker government and runs 13 years.
Signed on 3 January 2023, during the Donev caretaker government, with a term to 31 December 2035 - thirteen years.
Bulgaria pays about half a million euros a day under Botash.
The contract obliges Bulgargaz to pay BGN 1 million (EUR 512,000) per day for reserved capacity.
Botash exists because Petkov and Vasilev cut off Russian gas overnight, forcing an emergency solution.

Bulgargaz's own record states that Gazprom Export notified it on 26 April 2022 that supplies would be suspended 'despite the obligations to the Russian supplier for April 2022 having been fulfilled', with deliveries stopping at 07:00 on 27 April. The trigger was a supplier-side suspension, not a Bulgarian cutoff. The caretaker cabinet then signed Botash in January 2023, nine months later.
The causal story reverses who stopped the gas.
Bulgaria owes close to 400 million dollars and this will bankrupt Bulgargaz.

The prime minister put the liability at USD 360 million in July 2026 and arrears at about BGN 300 million in May 2026. 'Close to 400 million' rounds upward; the bankruptcy prediction is not established.
Depends on the currency: BTA's English rendering says USD 500,000 a day and nearly USD 400 million.
Gazprom, not the Bulgarian government, unilaterally stopped the supplies.
Bulgargaz records a unilateral suspension notice from Gazprom Export on 26 April 2022 effective 27 April.
The government reacted quickly and secured liquefied gas that could be delivered.
Emergency procurement is documented in outline; the speed and sufficiency of the replacement supply were not independently verified here.
Botash shows that one person can hold all power in the state.

This is an interpretive claim about decision-making concentration, not a checkable fact. What is documented is that the contract was signed by two state-owned companies' executives and never ratified by parliament.
Better treated as an argument than a claim.
Bulgaria will pay under this contract for thirteen years.
The term runs from 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2035.
The Botash deal was a decision of a caretaker government.
Signed 3 January 2023, during the Donev caretaker cabinet.
Under Botash Bulgaria pays 500,000 euros a day, unlike the Kyiv agreement.
The BGN 1 million daily capacity payment is EUR 512,000, which rounds to 500,000.
Bulgaria refused to join NATO's counter-drone programme.

On 11 September 2026 Defence Minister Stoyanov said Bulgaria would not join, citing a similar national capability; at the 14 October hearing he confirmed Bulgaria had not taken part 'from 2025 until now'.
True as of the debate; the accession note was signed the day after it.
The defence minister cited a price of 220,000 euros as too expensive.
Stoyanov told parliament on 14 October 2026 that the second project requires a mandatory annual contribution of EUR 220,000.
Bulgaria decided to join late, after the escalation.

The Council of Ministers approved accession on 28 October 2026 and the defence minister signed the note on 30 October - one day after the debate. 'Decided to join' was therefore true of the cabinet decision but not yet of the accession.
The government submitted the documents for participation in the programme.
The Council of Ministers approved the memorandum of understanding by protocol decision 46.32 on 28 October 2026, the day before the debate.
The minister stated the cost and Bulgaria nevertheless registered its participation.
The cost was stated and the cabinet approved accession, but the note of accession was signed on 30 October 2026, after the debate, and still required ratification.
Bulgaria participates in other systems such as IRIS.
Parliament approved an updated air-defence investment programme on 15 October 2026 covering IRIS-T, and the minister linked counter-drone procurement to that contract.
The defence minister refused inclusion in the system.
Same record: Stoyanov's 11 September 2026 refusal and his 14 October confirmation that Bulgaria had not taken part.
